2. Fiscal targets for end-June are on track to be met, supported by a pickup in revenues. Tax revenues grew by 11 percent y/y in real terms in May, marking the first positive real growth since August 2023. Stronger collection was explained by an uplift in the FX access tax (253 percent y/y), corporate income taxes (81 percent y/y), export duties (12 percent y/y), and adjustments to fuel taxes (7 percent y/y). Provincial co-participated revenues rose by 21 percent in real terms.

3. In line with program commitments, the authorities issued a resolution to raise electricity and gas prices and reduce the caps on subsidized consumption during S2:2024.

- Wholesale electricity and gas prices were raised in June to improve cost recovery, in the context of seasonally higher energy prices. The next adjustments are expected after August. Monthly caps on subsidized consumption of electricity (350 kWh) and gas were introduced for low-income households, and for medium-income households, the electricity cap was lowered (from 400 kWh to 250 kWh).
- Price increases were most pronounced for low-and-middle income households, where subsidies have been greatest,² and were implemented in the context where social benefits have been stepped up with improvements in their targeting.

On behalf of the Argentinean authorities, we thank Mr. Cubeddu, Mr. Ahuja, and the entire IMF mission team for the meaningful engagement and for the comprehensive and well-written staff report, and related material, on the Eighth Review under the Extended Fund Facility for Argentina.

My authorities have continued to deliver on their commitments to restore macro stability since the inauguration, further reaffirmed by the time of the seventh review, and as a result, the program is firmly on track. Moreover, the sizeable overperformance of all quantitative targets, as well as fulfilment of prior actions and structural benchmarks, are testament to the robust ownership and unwavering implementation of the stabilization plan.

Notably, Argentina's fiscal adjustment of almost 5 percent in the first few months of President Milei's administration ranks as one of the largest in all key programs with the IMF. This vital fiscal anchor, coupled with strict monetary discipline and a stable FX policy, are already bearing fruit with much faster-than-expected disinflation, reserve accumulation, and relative price realignment.

Additionally, recognizing the importance of the social safety net to also strengthen the viability of the stabilization plan, the authorities have scaled up meaningfully social benefits, as pensions are not only being preserved, but even increased in real terms.

Building upon these earlier-than-anticipated reassuring results, my authorities have also demonstrated agile policy making and, importantly, contingency planning, to secure the objectives of the program while addressing perennial macro imbalances. Against this backdrop, we concur with staff that enterprise risks to the Fund have declined.

Nevertheless, the road ahead is far from unchallenging since initial stability achievements still coexist with spotted fragility. The transition from the early corrective measures to a medium-term program, including by Congress approval of the landmark legislation Ley Bases and fiscal package, as anticipated, has proven lingering whilst the authorities fight vested interests across the board to streamline fiscal performance, stabilize the economy, and at the same time protect the most vulnerable, as it sets the grounds for an inclusive and sustained growth.

## Implementation of the stabilization plan

My authorities' have rapidly attained continued twin fiscal and current account

surpluses in the first five months of 2024, a fundamental stabilizing objective of the plan that accounts for the faster-than-expected stabilization signs, notably disinflation and reserve buildup.

**Frontloaded fiscal consolidation** of 5 percent of GDP as of end of April has allowed to bring monetary financing to a full stop at the wake of this administration, actually net credit to government became negative for about AR$1.5 trillion. This fiscal performance of a consecutive five-month overall surplus is unprecedented in the last decades; it stems from higher revenues, lower energy and transportation subsidies, discretionary spending cuts, public sector wage bill rationalization, capital expenditures streamlining, curbing of transfers to provinces and state-owned enterprises, and tighter management of decentralized public entities and trust funds. As of May 2024, tax collection was up 10.7 percent, while spending was down 27.6 percent, both in real terms; the fiscal primary surplus commitment for 2024 is 1.7 percent of GDP.

Going forward, my authorities are fully committed to transitioning to advanced quality measures, which are part of Ley Bases and the fiscal package that have already been passed by the lower house and are expected to be debated at the Senate in the coming days. Additionally, to further enhance tax revenues reducing distortionary taxes, a rate reduction of *impuesto PAIS* has been announced from 17.5 percent to 7.5 percent, once both legislation initiatives get Congress approval.

Plans continue to be developed, with technical assistance from the IMF, IDB, and World Bank, to improve tax compliance, rationalize the tax system, enhance the targeting of subsidies, improve the sustainability of the pension system, reinforce coordination at provincial levels, and improve governance of SOEs.

**Upscaled social spending** is also at the centerstage to protect the most vulnerable, and to safeguard the value of pensions in real terms; my authorities have more than doubled in real terms—compared to the previous year—the flagship child allowance program (AUH), as well as significantly increased spending in food stamp benefits (Alimentar & Primeros 1000 dias); while refining the targeting of other support and workfare programs like *Potenciar Trabajo*.

Importantly, **inflation** has sharply decreased to 8.8 percent in April 2024 from 25.5 percent in December 2023. Data for May 2024 will be released in the coming days; however, high frequency indicators show a further decline; there is no exact correlation, and only for reference, inflation in the city of Buenos Aires was 4.4 percent in May 2024, down from 9.8 percent in the previous month.

On the **exchange rate policy**, after the sharp initial step devaluation, followed by a consistent FX policy implementation, FX purchases amounted to USD17.2 billion since inauguration, also boosted by strong export recovery. Relatedly, Net International

Reserves (NIR) as of March 31 totaled USD8.7 billion, well above the USD6 billion target; furthermore, NIR accumulation since December 10, 2023 represented USD11.2 billion, even after addressing part of the FX backlog and a sizeable unwinding of the BIS swap. Remarkably, FX expectations derived from ROFEX futures contracts (t + 10 months) have had a downward evolution, with FX rates of 1,800 AR$/USD in December 2023, to 1,650 in February 2024, and 1,200 in May 2024.

Moreover, FX policy is expected to evolve consistently with the disinflation and reserve accumulation objectives. My authorities will continue to ease FX controls and unwind Multiple Currency Practice (MCPs) as conditions permit, and in transitioning to the new monetary regime "currency competition".

With regard to trade, goods trade reverted to a healthy surplus of USD7.2 billion from December 2023 to April 2024, compared to a deficit of minus USD8 billion in the period January-November 2023, representing a USD15.2 billion turnaround.

My authorities have also made important efforts to gradually normalize trade flows, with more than USD18 billion already tackled with the following breakdown: (i) BOPREAL subscription of USD10.1 billion, of which USD8.3 billion for legacy imports, and USD1.8 billion for dividend distribution abroad; (ii) MSMEs have already accessed USD700 million; and (iii) new imports reprofiling for USD7.1 billion.

Regarding monetary policy, its core objective remains disinflation, with a complementary anchoring role to enhance the fiscal stance. My authorities have continued to strengthen the central bank balance sheet; BCRA-remunerated liabilities are down to USD16 billion, 3.2 percent of GDP, from USD23 billion, 8.3 percent of GDP back in December 2023. The interest annual policy rate is down to 40 percent from 133 percent (a time when BCRA interest payments represented 10 percent of GDP).

Notably, the BCRA has published 2023 financial statements under new accounting standards more in line with international practice, marking at either fair value or amortized cost the non-transferable treasury bills and temporary advances to the government. Moreover, bank regulations are being gradually realigned for a better monetary transmission and improved credit allocation to the private sector.

On financing, a noteworthy net domestic financing of AR$24 trillion has been achieved through end May 2024 (3.9 percent of GDP) representing a rollover rate of 258 percent. Additionally, after successful conversion operations and new auctions, peso-denominated treasuries' maturities have been extended from an average duration of six months to three years, allowing not only to rebuild buffers, but also to buyback government debt held by the BCRA. At the same time, our engagement with multilateral and regional development banks has been intensified to mobilize net

positive financing, and we are working closely with all bilateral creditors to secure the delivery of committed financing.

The deep **structural reforms** laid out by the government aim at a market-oriented economy. They are designed to boost long-term investment and job creation and will not only expand Argentina's productive capacity and enhance external resilience, but also contribute to global energy security and climate goals. That will durably unlock Argentina's remarkable potential in energy, mining, technology, agriculture, and other strategic and export-oriented sectors, along with continued efforts to improve transparency and governance by further strengthening the AML/CFT framework in line with international standards. Improving Argentina's external sector, together with the pillars of the stabilization plan, is of utmost importance to improve the country's creditworthiness, as a pre-condition to gradually regain access to international capital markets by the end of next year.

## Conclusion

Argentina and its people are enduring a costly process towards stabilization, and inclusive and sustainable growth, to unlock the country and its people's massive potential. Challenges remain sizeable, however, and outstandingly, the majority of the people have sustained their support of President Milei's policies, actions, and vision. This vital social support continues to underpin the change mandate, and it will eventually drive the needed political support for the program.

My authorities reaffirm their commitment to the policies and objectives of the economic program supported by the IMF arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF), and to meeting the enhanced program's targets and structural conditionality for the remainder of the program. We also look forward to continuing to engage with the Fund as we develop our policies beyond this year and over the medium term.

Based on the steadfast implementation of the bold stabilization plan and our demonstrated strong commitment and ownership to the program, we encourage Executive Directors to support the eighth review under the extended arrangement under the EFF, the requests for approval of the modification of performance criteria to reflect program overperformance, a temporary exchange restriction, and multiple currency practices, and the financing assurances review.

metadata.title: IMF Staff Report: Argentina Eighth Review Under the Extended Fund Facility
metadata.summary:
This document package details the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) Eighth Review of Argentina's Extended Fund Facility (EFF) arrangement, dated June 2024, following discussions held in April-May 2024. The IMF Executive Board completed the review, enabling an $800 million disbursement, supporting Argentina's disinflation efforts, fiscal and external buffer rebuilding, and economic recovery. All end-March 2024 quantitative performance criteria were met, and waivers for exchange restrictions were approved.

The report highlights significant progress in Argentina's stabilization plan, driven by decisive policy actions, including fiscal and external surpluses, reserve accumulation, and reduced sovereign spreads. Monthly inflation has fallen below expectations, and the central bank's balance sheet has strengthened. Despite these achievements, significant imbalances and growth bottlenecks persist, necessitating further policy evolution. Key recommendations include enhancing the quality of fiscal adjustment through structural measures like personal income tax reform and subsidy rationalization, evolving monetary and FX policies towards positive real interest rates and greater flexibility, and implementing growth-unlocking reforms. The document also addresses the macroeconomic outlook, projecting a fall in monthly inflation, stable reserves, and sustained fiscal/external surpluses, while acknowledging elevated risks. It details supply-side policies aimed at correcting price misalignments and fostering a market-oriented economy through deregulation and eased FX restrictions. The report outlines ongoing efforts in social spending, debt management, and strengthening the banking system, and emphasizes the crucial need for securing key legislation to advance the reform agenda. It also provides a comprehensive table of contents and details figures, tables, and annexes included in the staff report.

outline.title: IMF Eighth Review: Overview, Progress, and Outlook (Pages 1-5)
outline.summary: This section provides an executive overview of the IMF's Eighth Review for Argentina under the EFF, detailing the $800 million disbursement, successful program performance against end-March 2024 quantitative criteria, and key policy priorities. It highlights significant progress in disinflation and fiscal balance achieved through decisive policy actions, while acknowledging persistent imbalances and growth bottlenecks. The section also covers Argentina's fiscal adjustment strategies, evolving monetary and FX policies, supply-side reforms, and the macroeconomic outlook, including projected inflation for end-2024 and an assessment of elevated yet more balanced risks.

subsections.title: IMF Executive Board Decision on Argentina's Eighth EFF Review, May 2024
subsections.summary: The IMF Executive Board completed Argentina's Eighth Review under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF), approving an $800 million disbursement. The program is on track, with all end-March 2024 quantitative performance criteria met, supporting Argentina's disinflation, fiscal and external buffer rebuilding, and recovery. Waivers for exchange restrictions were approved, and future steps include improving fiscal adjustment quality, evolving monetary/FX policies, and implementing growth-unlocking reforms.

subsections.title: Economic Program Assessment and Policy Enhancements for Argentina
subsections.summary: The IMF's assessment highlights Argentina's progress in disinflation and fiscal balance, meeting all end-March quantitative targets. However, persistent imbalances and growth bottlenecks necessitate enhanced policies, including improved fiscal adjustment quality (e.g., personal income tax reform, subsidy rationalization) and strengthened expenditure controls. Monetary and FX policies will evolve to include a positive real policy rate and a more flexible exchange rate to sustain disinflation and reserve accumulation.

subsections.title: Executive Summary: Argentina's Stabilization Plan Success and Persistent Imbalances
subsections.summary: Argentina's stabilization plan achieved fiscal and external surpluses, reserve accumulation, and reduced sovereign spreads, demonstrating decisive policy implementation. Despite this progress, significant imbalances and growth bottlenecks persist, requiring further policy evolution. The report notes efforts to build political support and scale up social assistance, while acknowledging market volatility due to legislative delays. Program performance is on track, with end-March quantitative criteria met and structural benchmarks progressing.

subsections.title: Argentina's Fiscal Adjustment, Monetary/FX Evolution, and Supply-Side Policies
subsections.summary: Argentina has achieved two-thirds of its planned fiscal consolidation through revenue measures and spending cuts, with anticipated legislative approval for further reforms. Monetary and FX policies will adapt to entrench disinflation and accumulate reserves, aiming for positive real interest rates and a more flexible exchange rate. Supply-side policies focus on correcting price misalignments and fostering a market-oriented economy through deregulation, which has shown positive initial impacts.

subsections.title: Macroeconomic Outlook and Risks for Argentina's Economy
subsections.summary: Monthly inflation in Argentina is projected to fall to 4% by end-2024, with reserves expected to remain stable due to offsetting capital inflows. Sustained fiscal and external surpluses are anticipated to strengthen reserves and market access. While risks remain elevated, they are more balanced post-stabilization. Downside risks include unfavorable external conditions, a protracted recession, and legislative delays, which may require further offsetting measures. Fund enterprise risks have moderated but remain significant.

outline.title: Report Structure and Contents (Pages 6-7)
outline.summary: This section details the structure of the IMF staff report on Argentina, identifying the key personnel involved in discussions during April-May 2024 and providing a comprehensive Table of Contents. It enumerates all figures, tables, annexes, and appendices, clarifying the data and analytical content available within the report, ranging from economic indicators and program performance to external sector analysis and a Letter of Intent.

subsections.title: IMF Staff, Officials Met, and Detailed Table of Contents (April-May 2024)
subsections.summary: This page lists the approving IMF staff (Rodrigo Valdés, Luis Cubeddu, Mark Flanagan) and the team involved in discussions held in Buenos Aires and Washington, D.C. during April-May 2024. It also includes key Argentine officials met, such as the Economy Minister and Central Bank President, and provides a detailed Table of Contents for the report, outlining sections like Context, Recent Developments, Program Performance, Strengthening the Stabilization Plan, Macroeconomic Outlook and Risks, Program Issues, Exceptional Access, and Staff Appraisal, along with a list of Boxes, Figures, Tables, Annexes, and Appendices.

subsections.title: Detailed List of Figures, Tables, Annexes, and Appendices
subsections.summary: This page provides a detailed list of Figures, Tables, Annexes, and Appendices included in the IMF staff report on Argentina. Figures cover performance relative to program targets, economic activity, inflation, market developments, fiscal/financing, and banking sector data. Tables present selected economic and financial indicators, balance of payments, government operations, central bank and banking sector operations, debt, financing needs, international investment position, and fund credit. Annexes address the external sector, debt sustainability, and the foreign exchange regime, while Appendices include a Letter of Intent.

outline.title: Recent Economic Developments and Program Performance (Pages 8-15)
outline.summary: This section details recent economic developments in Argentina and evaluates program performance. It highlights the success of the stabilization plan, including fiscal surpluses, reduced FX gaps, and significant reserve accumulation to US$0.3 billion by easing restrictions for MSMEs. Despite GDP contraction in Q4 2023 and Q1 2024, signs of stabilization are emerging. The section also covers improved debt management, sound banking sector financials, the impact of supply-side policies and deregulation, and confirmation that all end-March quantitative performance criteria were met, with net credit to the government remaining below zero and progress on structural benchmarks.

subsections.title: Context: Argentina's Stabilization Plan Success and Challenges (End-March QPC Met)
subsections.summary: This section, 'CONTEXT', highlights the success of Argentina's stabilization plan, driven by decisive policy actions leading to central bank FX purchases, consecutive fiscal surpluses, reduced FX gaps, and lower sovereign spreads. Monthly inflation fell below expectations, and the central bank's balance sheet strengthened. While FX restrictions have been eased and deregulation is improving resource allocation, the path remains challenging, requiring further adjustments to address legacy imbalances and growth bottlenecks. All quantitative performance criteria through end-March were met.

subsections.title: Economic Activity Contraction and Trade Balance Shift in Q4 2023 - Q1 2024
subsections.summary: Argentina's GDP fell sharply in Q4 2023 and Q1 2024 due to fiscal consolidation and price corrections, impacting private consumption and real wages. However, indicators like consumer confidence and credit show potential improvement starting in April. The trade balance shifted to a surplus, driven by import compression and export recovery, although the services deficit narrowed less significantly. The exchange rate appreciation has reached a medium-term equilibrium level.

subsections.title: Trade Balance Reversal and US$17 Billion FX Reserve Accumulation (Dec-Apr)
subsections.summary: Argentina experienced a significant trade balance reversal, with a cumulative goods trade surplus reaching US$7.2 billion from December to April, driven by reduced import volumes and an export rebound. The services deficit also narrowed. On a cash basis, the goods trade surplus was even higher due to commercial debt flows and private FX use for imports. Reserves are being replenished, with central bank FX purchases exceeding US$17 billion since mid-December, leading to a recovery in Net International Reserves (NIR).

subsections.title: Net International Reserve (NIR) Recovery to US$0.3 Billion and FX Access Easing
subsections.summary: Argentina's Net International Reserves (NIR) have recovered to approximately US$0.3 billion from a negative US$11.2 billion, supported by FX purchases and reduced private sector foreign asset purchases. This recovery allowed for the early elimination of FX access restrictions for MSMEs. Despite improvements, reserve coverage remains below 50% of the ARA metric, necessitating sustained strengthening, especially given future debt obligations. The full unwinding of the BIS credit facility in April is also noted.

subsections.title: Fiscal Policy Impact on Social Spending and Domestic Debt Management
subsections.summary: Argentina has protected real wages and pensions through adjustments like improved pension indexation. Strong fiscal and financing efforts have reduced domestic debt rollover risk, with a successful voluntary exchange extending maturities. Efforts are underway to shift towards fixed-rate instruments and unwind costly central bank options. Arrears have been maintained below the program ceiling, and efforts to clear arrears to CAMMESA are ongoing, supported by government transfers and gradual energy price convergence.

subsections.title: Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) 2023 Financial Reporting and Banking System Soundness
subsections.summary: The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) published its 2023 financial statements under new accounting policies, providing a more objective measure of its net equity. The banking system remains sound, well-capitalized, and liquid, despite increased public sector exposure. Private sector credit has contracted, but recovery signs are emerging. Profitability is stable, and asset quality has improved, with a decline in non-performing loans.

subsections.title: Supply-Side Policies, Price Misalignments, and Deregulation Impacts
subsections.summary: Argentina's supply-side policies aim to correct price misalignments and foster a market-oriented economy. Adjustments to energy and fuel prices align with international comparators, and wheat subsidies are phased out. The Emergency Decree (DNU) is improving resource allocation, leading to increased residential rental supply, lower real rates, and increased competition in air transport. Reduced import tariffs and streamlined customs procedures are expected to boost competition and productivity. Some FX restrictions have also been eased for MSMEs and specific goods.

subsections.title: Program Targets: Net Credit to Government and Structural Benchmarks (2024)
subsections.summary: This page confirms that net credit to the government remained below zero, with no direct monetary financing. It highlights the successful extension of domestic debt maturities through a voluntary exchange and the articulation of a strategy to enhance the monetary policy framework. Structural benchmarks include progress on easing FX controls. Figure 1 visually displays Argentina's performance relative to key program targets for Net International Reserves, Monetary Financing, Primary Balance, and Stock of Domestic Arrears as of specified dates in 2024.

outline.title: Strengthening Argentina's Stabilization Plan (Pages 16-22)
outline.summary: This section details the strategies for strengthening Argentina's stabilization plan, focusing on achieving a stronger fiscal anchor, improving monetary and FX frameworks, and removing growth bottlenecks. It outlines efforts to enhance the quality and durability of fiscal consolidation through structural measures, tax reforms, and subsidy rationalization by H2 2024. Reforms to public sector entities under Ley Bases, coupled with strict budget discipline and improved social assistance targeting, are also covered. The section further elaborates on the domestic and external financing strategy, the evolution towards a 'currency competition' monetary regime, streamlining banking regulations, structural policies for a market-oriented economy, and crucial reforms in the energy sector to enhance efficiency and governance.

subsections.title: Strategic Imperatives for Fiscal, Monetary, and Structural Reforms
subsections.summary: This section, 'STRENGTHENING THE STABILIZATION PLAN,' emphasizes the need for a stronger fiscal anchor, improved monetary and FX frameworks, and further steps to remove growth bottlenecks. Securing key legislation is crucial for the reform agenda. Delivering the planned fiscal consolidation for the year remains a top priority, requiring ambitious adjustment measures. Policy relies on higher-quality structural measures to safeguard against revenue risks. Successful stabilization episodes often involve similar magnitudes of fiscal consolidation, as noted in the comparison to cross-country examples.

subsections.title: Enhancing Fiscal Consolidation Quality and Subsidy Rationalization by H2 2024
subsections.summary: The authorities aim to achieve overall fiscal balance through structural measures, including potential revenue from a proposed fiscal package and rationalization of tax expenditures. Efforts to improve tax collection efficiency are ongoing, with plans to publish Compliance Risk Management tools. Subsidy rationalization, particularly in the energy sector, continues, with plans for full cost recovery for most users and a new tariff segmentation scheme supporting vulnerable households in the second half of 2024.

subsections.title: Public Sector Reforms, Budget Discipline, and Social Assistance Targeting
subsections.summary: This page stresses the importance of strong budget discipline and controls, outlining reforms in the proposed Ley Bases to rationalize public entities, strengthen public investment oversight, enhance employment flexibility, and repeal the pension moratorium. Ongoing efforts include improving cash management and consolidating government accounts. Enhancements in social assistance targeting and governance are also noted, focusing on means-tested programs for children and early childhood support, with efforts to improve governance by eliminating intermediaries and strengthening the social registry.

subsections.title: Domestic and External Financing Strategy for Debt Reduction and Market Access
subsections.summary: Argentina's domestic financing strategy focuses on reducing rollover risks and debt vulnerabilities, aiming for net peso debt placements at favorable rates and longer maturities, shifting from linked to fixed-rate bonds. Plans include broadening instruments, publishing an auction calendar, and deepening the investor pool. Steps are also being taken to replace central bank securities with Treasury securities to strengthen the BCRA's balance sheet. On the external front, preparations are underway for re-accessing international capital markets, with projected financing from official creditors.

subsections.title: Evolving Monetary and FX Policies Towards 'Currency Competition' Regime
subsections.summary: Argentina's central bank aims to evolve its monetary and FX policies towards a 'currency competition' regime. Key objectives include entrenching disinflation, building reserves by easing FX controls, maintaining price stability, prohibiting government financing, and acting as a lender of last resort. Accounting practices will shift to fair value. The transition period requires active monetary policy to anchor inflation expectations, supported by a fiscal anchor and limited credit.

subsections.title: Banking Regulation Streamlining and Structural Policies for Market-Oriented Economy
subsections.summary: Plans include streamlining banking regulations to enhance monetary transmission and private credit, ensuring a level playing field between traditional banks and Fintech companies. Macroprudential policies will prevent unhedged currency lending, and FX reserve requirements may act as liquidity buffers. Structural Policies emphasize a more open, market-oriented economy, with efforts to reduce import tariffs supporting competition, and price adjustments aligning protected sector prices more with international levels.

subsections.title: Energy Sector Reforms, Tariff Updates, and Governance Improvements
subsections.summary: This page focuses on improving efficiency and investment in Argentina's energy sector. Subsidies for energy production are being phased out, and tariffs for transportation and distribution have been significantly raised and are now automatically updated to reflect costs. Future pricing will align with cost recovery for households, supported by a new subsidy scheme. Reforms to the hydrocarbon sector's regulatory framework and pipeline expansion are crucial. Efforts to enhance transparency and governance in state functions, address corruption, and improve public spending controls are also highlighted.

outline.title: Macroeconomic Outlook, Risks, and Fund Engagement (Pages 23-25)
outline.summary: This section outlines Argentina's macroeconomic outlook, projecting a significant fall in inflation and a GDP contraction of 3.5% in 2024, followed by a 5% rebound in 2025. It details selected economic indicators from 2022-2025 and assesses the elevated but more balanced risks, including potential for recession, disinflation challenges, and legislative delays. The section also evaluates Fund-related financial, business, and reputational risks, noting improved manageability of obligations through late 2026 but highlighting continued challenges related to policy implementation, social conditions, and the need for sustained political support for reforms to achieve external viability.

subsections.title: Macroeconomic Projections: Inflation Fall, Surpluses, and 2024 GDP Contraction
subsections.summary: Inflation in Argentina is expected to fall in Q1 2024, supported by monetary/FX policy refinements and peso demand recovery. Medium-term fiscal and external surpluses are projected, ensuring debt sustainability and allowing for gradual easing of capital flow measures (CFMs). The economy is projected to contract by 3.5% in 2024, with recovery starting late 2024 due to market-oriented reforms, private investment, and fading fiscal headwinds. GDP growth is expected to rebound to around 5% next year, with monthly inflation reaching ~4% by end-2024.

subsections.title: Economic Indicators 2022-2025 and Elevated Risks Assessment
subsections.summary: This page presents Argentina's selected economic indicators from 2022-25, including GDP growth, inflation, and fiscal/external balances. It discusses elevated, though more balanced, risks, such as a protracted recession, stubborn disinflation, and social tensions. Delays in legislative approval and tightening global financial conditions pose challenges. Conversely, sustained market-oriented reforms could lead to a faster recovery. The authorities are prepared to implement contingency plans if risks materialize.

subsections.title: Fund-Related Financial, Business, and Reputational Risks Assessment
subsections.summary: Fund-related financial risks for Argentina have declined with the eighth review, making obligations manageable through late 2026. However, business risks persist due to large imbalances, policy implementation uncertainties, and maintaining societal support for reforms. Reputational risks have evolved, with the Fund's support for the current authorities alleviating evenhandedness concerns. The program relies on ambitious fiscal adjustment amid fragile social conditions, necessitating agile policymaking and social assistance. Restoring external viability hinges on political and societal support for reforms.

outline.title: Program Issues, Exceptional Access, and Staff Appraisal (Pages 26-32)
outline.summary: This section covers critical program issues for Argentina, including waivers for performance criteria nonobservance, corrective actions, and new structural benchmarks like tax system reform. It discusses projected reserve accumulation of US$5-12 billion annually and jurisdictional issues concerning Monetary and Credit Policy (MCPs) implemented post-February 2024. The section confirms the status of external arrears and Argentina's continued satisfaction of Exceptional Access criteria, while acknowledging elevated risks to debt sustainability. It highlights the importance of congressional approval for reforms, political fragmentation, and the staff's appraisal, which commends progress in macroeconomic stability, supports policy directions including 'currency competition,' and emphasizes the need for micro-level reforms and robust risk management.

subsections.title: Waivers, Corrective Actions, and New Structural Benchmarks
subsections.summary: This page addresses program issues, including a waiver for nonobservance of continuous performance criteria related to exchange restrictions, based on corrective actions like temporary maintenance of measures consistent with easing FX controls. Approval is sought to maintain temporary measures assessed as Monetary and Credit Policy (MCP) measures. A prior action involved removing wage indexation impacting utility bills. Proposed new structural benchmarks include developing a tax system reform proposal and an action plan to consolidate central government entities into a single treasury account.

subsections.title: Reserve Accumulation Targets and Jurisdictional Issues with MCPs (Post-Feb 2024)
subsections.summary: This page forecasts a gradual improvement in reserve coverage, accumulating US$5-12 billion annually, with potential upside from export growth. Full stabilization plan implementation is crucial to address balance of payments needs and remaining Fund obligations. Fund debt service will remain substantial post-2026. Jurisdictional issues are discussed regarding MCPs arising from exchange taxes and withholding taxes, with staff supporting temporary maintenance of these measures due to balance of payment reasons. The new MCP policy took effect on February 1, 2024.

subsections.title: External Arrears Status and Fulfillment of Exceptional Access Criteria
subsections.summary: This page details the status of Argentina's external arrears and litigation. Claims by YPFB for gas delivered in 2023 are being settled, and discussions are ongoing with Paraguay regarding overdue payments to Yacyreta. Two external arrears claims remain under litigation: Bpifrance Assurance Export and Titan Consortium I, LLC. The authorities confirmed no new external arrears were incurred since the seventh review. Staff assesses that Argentina continues to satisfy the four exceptional access (EA) criteria, contingent on continued implementation of the stabilization plan, despite elevated risks.

subsections.title: Debt Sustainability, Capital Market Access, and Safeguards Assessment
subsections.summary: This page discusses Argentina's debt servicing costs, maturity extensions, and capital controls, noting that the assessment of debt sustainability is subject to elevated risks and hinges on decisive implementation of the stabilization plan. Projected debt metrics remain above indicative targets, leaving limited maneuverability. Safeguards are in place for EA2. Criterion 3, regarding regaining access to private capital markets, is met, with external sovereign bond prices rising significantly due to policy implementation and improved market perception.

subsections.title: Congressional Approval, Implementation Risks, and Contingency Plans
subsections.summary: This page highlights ongoing efforts to secure congressional approval for fiscal and structural measures, with strong prospects for Senate approval. Passage of legislation would lay the foundation for higher-quality fiscal adjustment and economic turnaround. However, implementation risks persist due to political fragmentation and fragile social conditions. Contingency plans exist to achieve program objectives. The President's commitment to veto measures jeopardizing fiscal targets adds confidence to staff's assessment.

subsections.title: Staff Appraisal: Macroeconomic Stability and Policy Recommendations
subsections.summary: This page commends the authorities' actions to restore macroeconomic stability, including a four-month fiscal surplus and improved international reserves. Staff supports the plan to maintain an overall balance and begin unwinding distortive taxes, emphasizing the importance of reforms to tax, pension, and revenue-sharing systems. Progress in reducing domestic rollover risks and extending maturities is welcomed. Rebuilding external buffers is critical for re-accessing international capital markets by late 2025. Staff supports the transition to a new monetary regime with 'currency competition'.

subsections.title: Staff Appraisal: Micro-Level Reforms and Program Risk Management
subsections.summary: This page stresses the need for micro-level reforms to support recovery and boost potential growth, including securing approval for the Ley Bases legislation. These reforms aim to eliminate entry barriers, increase labor market flexibility, modernize the hydrocarbons framework, and incentivize investment. Enhancing transparency and governance, including a comprehensive assessment and strengthening the AML/CFT framework, is also recommended. Program risks remain elevated, requiring continued commitment and adaptation of policies, with authorities ready to implement contingency plans.

outline.title: Thematic Deep Dives: Boxes 1-6 (Pages 33-39)
outline.summary: This section provides six thematic deep dives into key aspects of Argentina's economic and social landscape. It covers the deterioration of social conditions, rising poverty to 42% by mid-2023, and challenges in provincial finances with intergovernmental imbalances. The section also presents lessons from successful stabilization programs, highlighting the importance of fiscal consolidation and flexible FX regimes. Furthermore, it analyzes the impacts and legal status of the Emergency Decree Bill (DNU) and Ley Bases reform, details the evolution of Argentina's Net International Investment Position (NIIP) from 2016-2023, and addresses the significant US$21 billion FX debt backlog and overhang as of April 2024.

subsections.title: Box 1: Argentina's Social Conditions and Welfare Challenges (2023)
subsections.summary: Box 1 discusses Argentina's social conditions, noting a deterioration over the past decade with poverty rising to 42% by mid-2023 and growing inequality, particularly for children. Key drivers include lackluster growth, informality, and declining real wages. While social safety net coverage is comprehensive, assistance often lags inflation, creating gaps. Governance issues persist, with some programs lacking effective targeting. The section describes the evolution of social conditions under the Milei administration.

subsections.title: Box 2: Provincial Finances, Intergovernmental Transfers, and Fiscal Discipline
subsections.summary: Box 2 examines Argentina's provincial finances, highlighting persistent imbalances between subnational government spending (education, healthcare, security) and revenue. A complex system of intergovernmental transfers exists, including automatic and discretionary transfers. These imbalances weaken fiscal discipline, as provinces have weak incentives to improve revenue collection and spending often follows available funds plus transfers. The federal government relies on distortive taxes and discretionary transfers. Recent developments since 2016-19 are discussed, including a fiscal pact.

subsections.title: Box 3: Lessons from Successful and Unsuccessful Stabilization Programs (10-Year Review)
subsections.summary: Box 3 draws lessons from successful and unsuccessful stabilization programs, suggesting that success involves larger, frontloaded fiscal consolidation, earlier transition to flexible FX regimes with inflation targets, and structural policy support. Achieving results takes time and requires adaptation. Successful episodes featured substantial fiscal adjustments (e.g., +6 ppts of GDP in Peru), often calibrated to rule out monetary financing, with central bank charter changes introduced later. Durable measures were implemented over time to enhance credibility. The box presents figures comparing key macroeconomic variables in successful vs. unsuccessful programs, showing tighter fiscal policy, quicker monetary normalization, and sustained reserve accumulation in successful cases. Reducing inflation to low levels took time.

subsections.title: Box 4: Emergency Decree Bill (DNU) and Landmark Reform Law (Ley Bases)
subsections.summary: Box 4 discusses the Emergency Decree Bill (DNU) and the Landmark Reform Law (Ley Bases) in Argentina. The DNU aims to deregulate the economy and enhance competition but faces legal challenges and Senate rejection. The Ley Bases, passed by the lower chamber, includes wide-ranging market-based reforms and is expected to strengthen the DNU's legal basis. Summaries of the DNU's reform clauses and the Ley Bases' main provisions are presented in tables.

subsections.title: Box 5: Evolution of Argentina's Net International Investment Position (NIIP) 2016-2023
subsections.summary: Box 5 analyzes the evolution of Argentina's Net International Investment Position (NIIP) from 2016-2023. Despite a positive NIIP, external vulnerabilities remain high due to mismatched asset/liability composition. The NIIP doubled between 2016-19 due to private sector asset growth outpacing public external debt. Since 2019, the net position stabilized, but gross assets/liabilities shifted. Private sector assets abroad increased, while private liabilities rose, partly due to FX restrictions on imports.

subsections.title: Box 6: Argentina's FX Debt Backlog and Overhang (US$21 Billion as of April 2024)
subsections.summary: Box 6 assesses Argentina's FX debt backlog and overhang, totaling roughly US$21 billion as of end-April 2024, including excess importers' debt and undistributed dividends. Approximately US$17 billion has been reprofiled through BOPREAL schemes and delayed FX access for new imports. Achieving reserve accumulation goals requires sustained tight policies and enhanced monetary/FX management. Delayed FX access for imports will likely be necessary to manage the country's payment obligations.

outline.title: Key Economic Trends and Market Indicators (Visuals) (Pages 40-44)
outline.summary: This section visually analyzes key economic trends and market indicators in Argentina, covering the sharp contraction in economic activity from Q4 2023, improved trade balance due to import compression and agricultural export recovery, and stable employment. It details the sharp decrease in headline inflation post-December spike, attributed to currency crawl and declining expectations, along with a real decrease in central bank liabilities. Market developments show increased FX purchases, narrowed FX gaps, reduced sovereign spreads, and significant real exchange rate appreciation. The section highlights fiscal surpluses from January-April 2024 due to spending cuts and the halt of monetary financing, concluding with an assessment of growing banking sector liquidity, sound capitalization, falling NPLs, but weak private credit due to negative real interest rates.

subsections.title: Economic Activity, Trade Balance, and Employment Trends (Q4 2023)
subsections.summary: This page discusses Argentina's economic activity and trade balance. It highlights a sharp contraction in economic activity led by the non-agricultural sector starting in Q4 2023, while real wages appear to be bottoming out. The trade balance has improved due to import compression and increased exports, primarily from the agricultural sector's recovery. Employment indicators remained stable through end-2023. The section continues a discussion on economic trends with charts illustrating economic activity and its components.

subsections.title: Inflation Dynamics, Monetary Indicators, and Central Bank Liabilities
subsections.summary: This page focuses on inflation trends in Argentina, noting a sharp decrease in sequential headline inflation after a December spike. This decline is attributed to a low rate of currency crawl and falling inflation expectations, although expectations remain elevated. The central bank's liabilities have decreased in real terms, and declining policy rates are strengthening its balance sheet. Money demand and supply have also fallen sharply. This page continues the discussion on inflation with charts showing headline and core inflation.

subsections.title: Market Developments: FX Gap, Sovereign Spreads, and Real Exchange Rate
subsections.summary: This page details Argentina's recent market developments, indicating that the stabilization plan has led to increased FX purchases, a narrowed FX gap (though widening recently due to political uncertainty), reduced sovereign spreads, and lower devaluation expectations. The real exchange rate has appreciated significantly, while policy rates remain negative in real terms. The page includes charts on FX intervention and other market indicators, continuing the analysis of economic stabilization.

subsections.title: Fiscal and Financing Developments: Consecutive Surpluses (Jan-Apr 2024) and Monetary Financing Halt
subsections.summary: This page presents Argentina's fiscal and financing developments, highlighting consecutive fiscal surpluses in January-April 2024, the first in over a decade. This improvement is driven by significant real spending cuts, which have also halted monetary financing. Cash management has improved, and primary bond issuances are being used to sterilize BCRA purchases and extend debt maturities. The page includes charts on overall deficit as a percentage of GDP, indicating a positive fiscal trend for 2024.

subsections.title: Banking Sector Liquidity, Capitalization, and Credit Trends
subsections.summary: This page discusses the liquidity buffers and banking sector in Argentina. Liquidity buffers are growing, and nominal lending and deposit rates are declining in line with monetary policy. Banks maintain high exposure to the public sector, but capitalization remains sound and non-performing loans (NPLs) are falling. However, negative real interest rates have caused a marked decline in real peso time deposits, and private credit remains weak. Charts illustrate domestic and foreign currency liquidity in the banking sector.

outline.title: Annex Tables: Economic & Financial Data 2022-2029 (Pages 45-50)
outline.summary: This section comprises a series of detailed annex tables providing comprehensive economic and financial data for Argentina from 2017 to 2032. It includes Table 1 (selected indicators), Table 2 (external balance of payments), Table 3a and 3b (Federal Government Operations), Table 4 (General Government Operations), Table 5a (Central Bank Operations), Table 5b (Banking Sector Operations), Table 6 (Public and External Debt), Table 7 (Federal Government Gross Financing Needs), Table 8 (External Gross Financing Needs), Table 9 (Federal Government Debt by Creditor), Table 10 (International Investment Position), Table 11 (Financial Soundness Indicators), and Table 12 (Indicators of Fund Credit). Each table includes specific notes clarifying definitions, assumptions, and components for in-depth analysis of Argentina's projected and historical economic and financial performance.

subsections.title: Table 1: Selected Economic and Financial Indicators for Argentina 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 45 contains Table 1, which provides selected economic and financial indicators for Argentina from 2022 to 2029. It includes data on GDP growth, inflation, fiscal balances, current account, and gross financing needs. The table also details specific notes regarding revenue definitions, spending components, and balance calculations, serving as a key reference for projected economic performance.

subsections.title: Table 2: Argentina's External Balance of Payments 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 46 presents Table 2, detailing Argentina's external balance of payments from 2022 to 2029. It covers various components of the current and capital accounts, including trade balance, income, current transfers, foreign direct investment (FDI), portfolio investment, and other investment. The table also outlines gross financing needs and sources, providing a comprehensive outlook on Argentina's external financial position and projections.

subsections.title: Table 3a: Federal Government Operations in ARS Billions 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 47 provides Table 3a, showing Argentina's Federal Government Operations in billions of Argentine Pesos from 2022 to 2029. It details revenues, expenditures, and different measures of fiscal balance, including primary and overall balances. The table includes specific notes on revenue definitions, transfers, deposit accumulation, debt repayment assumptions, and various components of federal government financing, offering a detailed fiscal breakdown.

subsections.title: Table 3b: Federal Government Operations as Percentage of GDP 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 48 contains Table 3b, presenting Argentina's Federal Government Operations as a percentage of GDP from 2022 to 2029. It mirrors the data in Table 3a but normalizes it by GDP, allowing for analysis of fiscal trends in relation to economic size. Specific notes clarify revenue components, transfers, debt assumptions, and adjustments for economic cycles and one-off events, crucial for understanding fiscal policy impacts.

subsections.title: Table 4: General Government Operations as Percentage of GDP 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 49 presents Table 4, outlining Argentina's General Government Operations (including federal and provincial governments) from 2022 to 2029. It provides data on fiscal balances, revenue, and expenditure components, both in percentage of GDP and adjusted for economic cycles. The table specifies the scope of general government, exclusions from primary balance, and definitions of overall balance, offering a consolidated view of public finances.

subsections.title: Table 5a: Central Bank (BCRA) Operations 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 50 includes Table 5a, summarizing the operations of Argentina's Central Bank (BCRA) from 2022 to 2029. It covers balance sheet items, profit distribution, net interest margin, and financing operations. Specific notes clarify valuation methods, assumptions on profit distribution, definitions of net interest margin, and adjustments for treasury buybacks and liquidity issuance, providing insights into the BCRA's financial activities and projections.

subsections.title: Table 5b: Banking Sector Operations 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 51 presents Table 5b, summarizing Argentina's Banking Sector operations from 2022 to 2029, detailing deposits, credit, liquidity, and capitalization, including the definition of Private M3*.

subsections.title: Table 6: Public and External Debt 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 52 contains Table 6, summarizing Argentina's public and external debt from 2022 to 2029 in billions of U.S. dollars, broken down by domestic currency, foreign currency, external debt, BCRA swap lines, and provincial governments, with notes on exchange rate impact and debt buybacks.

subsections.title: Table 7: Federal Government Gross Financing Needs and Sources 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 53 provides Table 7, detailing Argentina's Federal Government Gross Financing Needs and Sources from 2022 to 2029 in millions of U.S. dollars, outlining domestic and external financing, BCRA, public entities, and assumptions for rollover and interest capitalization.

subsections.title: Table 8: External (Residency) Gross Financing Needs and Sources 2022-2029
subsections.summary: Page 54 presents Table 8, outlining Argentina's External (Residency) Gross Financing Needs and Sources from 2022 to 2029 in millions of U.S. dollars, detailing external financing sources, including official loans, private sector debt, and reserve changes.

subsections.title: Table 9: Federal Government Debt by Creditor 2017-2023
subsections.summary: Page 55 contains Table 9, showing Argentina's Federal Government Debt by Creditor from 2017 to 2023, categorizing debt by domestic and external creditors, including the Paris Club, private sector, and public sector entities like BCRA and FGS.

subsections.title: Table 10: International Investment Position 2018-2023
subsections.summary: Page 56 presents Table 10, detailing Argentina's International Investment Position from 2018 to 2023, including data on direct investment, portfolio investment, financial derivatives, other investment, and reserve assets, categorized by assets and liabilities.

subsections.title: Table 11: Financial Soundness Indicators 2017-2023
subsections.summary: Page 57 includes Table 11, listing Argentina's Financial Soundness Indicators from 2017 to 2023, covering capital adequacy, asset quality (NPLs), profitability, and liquidity for the banking sector, with a note on inflation-adjusted NPLs from 2020.

subsections.title: Table 12: Indicators of Fund Credit 2024-2032
subsections.summary: Page 58 presents Table 12, detailing Indicators of Fund Credit for Argentina from 2024 to 2032 in millions of SDRs, outlining projected purchases, repurchases, and outstanding amounts related to the IMF, assuming all intended purchases are made.

outline.title: IMF Program Specific Tables & Annex I: External Sector Assessment (Pages 59-61)
outline.summary: This section presents specific tables related to IMF program performance criteria and introduces Annex I, providing an external sector assessment with references to tables 24 and 25.

subsections.title: Fund Staff Calculations: Performance Criteria (Page 59)
subsections.summary: Page 59 contains a table related to Fund staff calculations, outlining periodic and continuous performance criteria for Argentina, indicating ongoing compliance requirements for the financial program.

subsections.title: Annex I: External Sector Assessment (Tables 24 & 25) (Pages 60-61)
subsections.summary: Pages 60 and 61 introduce Annex I, focusing on the External Sector Assessment, with explicit references to Table 24 and Table 25, which likely contain detailed data relevant to Argentina's external financial position.

outline.title: Annex II: Sovereign Risk and Debt Sustainability Framework (SRDSF) 2014-2033 (Pages 62-73)
outline.summary: This comprehensive section details Argentina's Sovereign Risk and Debt Sustainability Framework, assessing debt sustainability, medium- and longer-term risks, key macroeconomic assumptions, and providing various tables on debt coverage, structure, baseline scenarios, and risk analysis from 2014 to 2033.

subsections.title: DSA Summary Assessment: Debt Sustainability & Risks (Pages 62-63)
subsections.summary: Pages 62-63 introduce Annex II and the Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA) Summary Assessment, concluding that Argentina's debt is sustainable but not with high probability, with overall risks identified as high. It outlines the four assessment tools used and emphasizes that the assessment hinges on the successful implementation of the stabilization plan, including a strong fiscal anchor and FX regime realignment.

subsections.title: Medium-Term Risk Analysis (GFN Financeability Module, 9% GDP) & Contingent Liabilities (Pages 64-65)
subsections.summary: Pages 64-65 detail the medium-term risk analysis, showing moderate risk according to the GFN Financeability Module (average GFNs of 9% of GDP). It discusses vulnerabilities like high financial dollarization and the importance of a fiscal anchor. The analysis also covers contingent liabilities from international court rulings and provincial debt, stressing agile policymaking for medium-term debt sustainability and introducing longer-term risk analysis with an 86% probability of debt stabilization by 2033.

subsections.title: Box 1: SRDSF Key Macroeconomic and Financing Assumptions (2024 GDP Contraction, 2.4% Medium-Term Growth) (Pages 66-67)
subsections.summary: Pages 66-67 present Box 1, outlining the SRDSF's key macroeconomic and financing assumptions. These include the Milei administration's fiscal commitment, a projected 3.5% real GDP contraction in 2024 followed by 2.4% medium-term growth, and an initial REER depreciation. It also covers domestic market financing, a shift from inflation-linked to fixed-rate instruments, rising real interest rates, and significant financing risks due to policy uncertainty.

subsections.title: Table 2: Debt Coverage and Disclosures (Excluding GDP Warrants, Provincial Debt) (Page 68)
subsections.summary: Page 68 presents Table 2, "Argentina: Debt Coverage and Disclosures," which clarifies the scope of the SRDSA. It defines various debt terms and explicitly states the exclusion of items like GDP warrants and provincial debt, focusing on central government debt held by private, official, and public sectors.

subsections.title: Table 3: Public Debt Structure Indicators 2014-2033 (Page 69)
subsections.summary: Page 69 displays Table 3, "Argentina: Public Debt Structure Indicators," featuring charts illustrating debt by currency, holder, governing law, instruments, and maturity as percentages of GDP from 2014 to 2033. It highlights the dominance of foreign-currency denominated debt and initial reliance on CER-linkers, noting mitigation of rollover risks by IFI-held FX debt and intra-public sector holdings.

subsections.title: Table 4: Realism of Baseline Assumptions (Page 70)
subsections.summary: Page 70 presents Table 4, "Argentina: Realism of Baseline Assumptions," including charts on public debt creating flows, 3-year debt reduction, fiscal adjustment, possible growth paths, and real GDP growth. It comments on the optimism of baseline forecasts for debt reduction and exchange rate paths, acknowledging exceptionally high risks given Argentina's economic volatility.

subsections.title: Table 5: Baseline Scenario: Public Debt Projections & Contribution (Page 71)
subsections.summary: Page 71 presents Table 5, "Argentina: Baseline Scenario," with charts on "Contribution to Change in Public Debt" and "Public Debt." It indicates a projected long-term decline in public debt due to fiscal anchor adherence and lower FX misalignments, stressing the importance of domestic capital markets and exports, and explains 2023-2024 residuals by stock-flow adjustments from exchange rate volatility and reduced effective interest rates.

subsections.title: Table 6: Medium-Term Risk Analysis (Page 72)
subsections.summary: Page 72 presents Table 6, "Argentina: Medium-Term Risk Analysis," including charts for the Final Fanchart, Gross Financing Needs, and Medium-Term Index. The analysis identifies a high medium-term risk due to fanchart widening from valuation effects, but assesses overall risk as moderate due to expected declines in debt-to-GDP ratios, emphasizing fiscal anchor adherence for containing financing risks amid substantial uncertainty.

subsections.title: Table 7: Decomposition of Public Debt & Debt Service by Creditor 2024-2025 (Page 73)
subsections.summary: Page 73 presents Table 7, "Argentina: Decomposition of Public Debt and Debt Service by Creditor for 2024–2025." It details debt classifications by official, commercial, multilateral, and bilateral creditors, with footnotes clarifying definitions and coverage, noting the exclusion of holdouts from this specific table while maintaining consistency with the DSA's debt coverage.

outline.title: Annex III: Foreign Exchange Regime Assessment & Multiple Currency Practices (Pages 74-77)
outline.summary: This section, Annex III, provides an assessment of Argentina's foreign exchange regime, focusing on exchange restrictions and multiple currency practices (MCPs). It details the evolution of these practices, including the introduction of new restrictions, modifications to existing ones, and the impact of instruments like BOPREAL and Impuesto Pais taxes, explaining how they create MCPs and exchange restrictions.

subsections.title: Overview of Exchange Restrictions & Multiple Currency Practices (Page 74)
subsections.summary: Page 74 introduces Annex III, which addresses Argentina's Foreign Exchange Regime, focusing on exchange restrictions and multiple currency practices (MCPs). It notes the identification of several such practices upon the approval of the extended arrangement, their subsequent modification, and the introduction of new ones, providing an updated assessment.

subsections.title: BOPREAL Instrument, Impuesto Pais Tax & MCP Formation (Page 75)
subsections.summary: Page 75 continues the FX regime discussion, detailing the BOPREAL instrument for dividend payments and adjustments to the Impuesto Pais tax, including its increase and extension to BOPREAL subscriptions. These measures result in the creation of a multiple currency practice (MCP) and an exchange restriction.

subsections.title: Specific Exchange Restrictions & Exchange Taxes (Page 76)
subsections.summary: Page 76 details specific exchange restrictions maintained by Argentina, such as limitations on current account transfers for remittances, medical, and educational expenses, and requirements for external loan payments. It also begins listing exchange taxes, including a 30% tax on foreign exchange purchases for individuals and luxury goods.

subsections.title: Assessment of Multiple Currency Practices (MCPs) Under IMF Policy (Page 77)
subsections.summary: Page 77 continues the assessment of exchange restrictions and MCPs under the new IMF policy. It explains how official actions creating impermissible exchange rate spreads lead to MCPs, specifically identifying several arising from exchange taxes, including varying rates on foreign exchange purchases for travel, luxury goods, and professional/other services.

outline.title: Letter of Intent and Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (MEFP) (May 31, 2024) (Pages 78-88)
outline.summary: This section comprises Argentina's Letter of Intent to the IMF (May 31, 2024) and the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (MEFP) update. It outlines the government's successful efforts in restoring macroeconomic stability, disinflation, reserve accumulation, and fiscal surplus, while detailing ongoing and future policy commitments across fiscal, monetary, FX, and structural reforms to sustain progress and ensure economic recovery from 2024 onwards.

subsections.title: Letter of Intent to IMF Managing Director (May 31, 2024) (Pages 78-79)
subsections.summary: Pages 78-79 contain Argentina's Letter of Intent, dated May 31, 2024, to IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. It highlights the administration's success in averting crisis, restoring stability, achieving fiscal surplus, halting central bank financing, disinflation, and reserve accumulation. The letter requests completion of the Eighth Review, disbursement of SDR 600 million, and approval for target modifications and waivers.

subsections.title: Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (MEFP) Update: Macroeconomic Stability & Social Support (May 31, 2024) (Pages 80-81)
subsections.summary: Pages 80-81 present an update to the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (MEFP), dated May 31, 2024. It highlights successful policy actions leading to macroeconomic stability, sustained fiscal surplus, increased reserves, reduced inflation, improved market indicators, and enhanced social support for vulnerable populations. It also notes stabilizing economic activity, recovering real wages, rapid disinflation (8.8% in April), strengthening central bank balance sheet, and significant external surpluses and reserve accumulation (US$15.5 billion trade surplus Dec-Apr).

subsections.title: Prudent Public Debt Management & Market-Based Economy Reforms (Page 82)
subsections.summary: Page 82 discusses Argentina's prudent public debt management, including successful net placements, reduced rollover risks, and a debt exchange extending 40% of peso debt. It outlines the strategy for new short-term fixed-rate instruments to shift liquidity from BCRA and maintain net-zero monetary financing. The page also details efforts to deregulate the economy, correct regulated utility and fuel prices, eliminate wheat price subsidies, and improve resource allocation through an Emergency Decree.

subsections.title: Economic Projections: Inflation Convergence & External Surpluses (2024) (Page 83)
subsections.summary: Page 83 outlines economic projections, forecasting inflation to converge to around 4% monthly by end-2024, supported by a strong fiscal anchor, cessation of debt monetization, and a strengthened monetary/FX policy framework. The external current account is expected to shift to a 0.6% of GDP surplus this year, with long-term external surpluses and a US$7 billion increase in reserve accumulation projected for 2024.

subsections.title: Policy Commitments: Contingency Measures & FX Policy Adjustments (Page 84)
subsections.summary: Page 84 details the government's commitment to adapt economic policies, safeguarding credibility through a strong fiscal anchor and reserve accumulation goals. It lists contingency measures, including strengthening excises, accelerating subsidy reductions, streamlining transfers, and enhancing tax administration. On monetary and FX policy, the government is prepared to adjust ex-ante real policy interest rates sooner if inflation proves challenging, supported by clear communication.

subsections.title: Fiscal Policy Goals: Overall Balance 2024, Subsidy Reduction & Social Safeguards (Page 85)
subsections.summary: Page 85 outlines fiscal policy goals, aiming for overall balance in 2024 through improved tax progressivity, reduced subsidies (energy and transportation by at least 0.7% of GDP), and strengthened expenditure controls, while safeguarding social assistance. It details plans for achieving full cost recovery for most energy users by S2:2024 and the issuance of a decree removing the CVS formula for utility bills.

subsections.title: Tax System Reform, Pension Sustainability & Financing Strategy (Page 86)
subsections.summary: Page 86 details plans to enhance the tax system's efficiency, equity, and simplicity by October 2024, including reducing distortive taxes like 'impuesto pais' by end-2024. Complementary reforms will focus on pension system sustainability, fiscal frameworks, and intergovernmental transfers, with a roadmap by end-2024. Financing strategy includes tapping the domestic debt market, offering diverse instruments, and gradually replacing FX- and inflation-linked bonds with fixed-rate securities.

subsections.title: Monetary & FX Policy Framework Evolution (Page 87)
subsections.summary: Page 87 discusses the evolution of monetary and FX policy, affirming that the overnight policy interest rate will continue to guide inflation expectations and address quasi-fiscal deficits. The real policy rate is expected to turn positive later in the year. Plans include extending monetary operations to include Treasuries, prohibiting BCRA profit transfers to the Treasury, refining accounting standards, and adopting a more flexible FX policy to support reserve buildup and disinflation.

subsections.title: Proposed Law for Employment, Investment & SOE Reforms (Page 88)
subsections.summary: Page 88 outlines a proposed law, pending Congressional approval, aimed at supporting private formal employment, incentivizing long-term investments, strengthening the hydrocarbon sector, streamlining regulatory costs, and rationalizing state-owned enterprises (SOEs), including privatization processes. Post-approval, focus will shift to implementation, improving efficiency in key sectors, unwinding cross-subsidies, and strengthening AML/CFT frameworks.

outline.title: Quantitative Performance Criteria & Technical Memorandum of Understanding (TMU) (May 31, 2024) (Pages 89-99)
outline.summary: This section provides the Quantitative Performance Criteria and Indicative Targets for Argentina's program, alongside the Technical Memorandum of Understanding (TMU). The TMU, dated May 31, 2024, defines the metrics, assessment methods, and information requirements for monitoring program performance, including specific definitions for primary balance, domestic arrears, gross official reserve liabilities, BCRA's net financing, and debt for program purposes.

subsections.title: Table 1: Quantitative Performance Criteria & Indicative Targets (Pages 89-91)
subsections.summary: Pages 89-91 refer to Table 1, "Argentina: Quantitative Performance Criteria and Indicative Targets," which outlines program-specific performance criteria and indicative targets. Although the table content is external, these pages provide definitions, sources, program exchange rates (December 29, 2023), flow definitions, reserve targets, and adjustors, crucial for monitoring program compliance.

subsections.title: Additional Program Data Tables (Pages 92-93)
subsections.summary: Pages 92-93 contain references to additional tables ([tbl-39.md] and [tbl-40.md]), which likely provide further tabular data relevant to the document's economic and financial policies update and program monitoring.

subsections.title: Attachment II: Technical Memorandum of Understanding (TMU) Update (May 31, 2024) (Page 94)
subsections.summary: Page 94 introduces "Attachment II. Technical Memorandum of Understanding Update," dated May 31, 2024. It outlines definitions for performance criteria (PCs) and indicative targets (ITs), methods for assessing program performance, and information requirements, establishing program exchange rates from December 29, 2023.

subsections.title: TMU: Definition of Federal Government Primary Balance (Page 95)
subsections.summary: Page 95 details the TMU's definition of the federal government's primary balance according to 'Esquema IMIG' and 2014 GFS Manual practices. It specifies revenue inclusions (tax, property, other current, capital) and exclusions (financial transfers from BCRA, interest from intra-public sector holdings, asset sale proceeds, licenses, debt issuance, SDRs) for primary deficit calculations.

subsections.title: TMU: Measurement of Federal Government Primary Balance & Domestic Arrears (Page 96)
subsections.summary: Page 96 details the TMU's measurement of the Federal government's cumulative primary balance and defines domestic arrears as floating debt (difference between accrual and cash basis primary spending). It establishes a ceiling for the daily average of domestic arrears over the final two weeks of each quarter (0.8% of GDP), requiring daily data submission to the Fund.

subsections.title: TMU: Definition of Gross Official Reserve Liabilities (Page 97)
subsections.summary: Page 97 defines Gross official reserve liabilities in foreign currencies for program monitoring, including short-term liabilities and net deliverable forward FX liabilities. It clarifies exclusions (Federal government's foreign liabilities, FX deposits at BCRA) and notes various BCRA liabilities (swaps with China, bank reserve requirements, etc.), with cumulative change in Net International Reserves (NIR) monitored daily from December 10, 2023.

subsections.title: TMU: Ceiling on BCRA's Net Financing of Federal Government (Page 98)
subsections.summary: Page 98 defines the ceiling on the BCRA's Net Financing of the Federal Government, encompassing various forms of financing like overdrafts, profit distributions, and government debt acquisition. Net financing deducts cash transfers for security repurchases or overdraft reductions, excluding debt exchanges. The cumulative flow ceiling for net financing in 2024 is set at zero.

subsections.title: TMU: Definition of Debt for Program Purposes (Page 99)
subsections.summary: Page 99 provides the TMU's detailed definitions of debt for program purposes, including obligations such as repurchase agreements, official swap arrangements, suppliers' credits, and leases. It specifies that arrears, penalties, and damages from unpaid debt are considered debt, aligning the definition of external debt with the IMF's Balance of Payments Manual.

outline.title: Argentina's Economic Data Reporting Requirements
outline.summary: This section consolidates the detailed reporting requirements for Argentina's economic monitoring, covering quantitative targets for social assistance programs, daily economic variables, weekly and fortnightly financial data, monthly fiscal financing and federal debt, and quarterly provincial debt statistics and projections.

subsections.title: Daily and Quantitative Target Data Reporting
subsections.summary: This section defines variables for quantitative targets related to federal government social assistance programs (e.g., Asignación Universal para Protección Social, Tarjeta Alimentar, Progresar), with data due within 25 days of month-end. It also details daily data submissions for key economic variables including exchange rates, BCRA currency issued, bank deposits, liquidity assistance, interest rates, BCRA's international reserves, and banks' foreign exchange positions.

subsections.title: Weekly and Fortnightly Economic Data Reporting
subsections.summary: This section outlines weekly reporting requirements, which include the BCRA balance sheet, BCRA-issued securities data, BOPREAL stock and maturity, and daily securities trading data. Fortnightly reports cover domestic debt instrument interest rates and provide information on outstanding local and global debt, including maturity, currency, and holders. It also indicates the commencement of monthly reporting for federal government operations and cash flow.

subsections.title: Monthly Fiscal Financing and Federal Debt Reporting
subsections.summary: This section details monthly reporting requirements for Argentina's fiscal financing, covering sources like BCRA transfers, debt issuance, and external financing, with a 25-day lag, alongside a quarterly financing plan. It also includes monthly federal debt service (amortization and interest) for domestic and external debt, projected payments, and information on guaranteed debt. External arrears are reported continuously, and federal debt stock by currency is provided monthly.

subsections.title: Quarterly Provincial Debt Reporting and Projections
subsections.summary: This section specifies quarterly reporting for provincial government debt, encompassing stock data by currency, creditor, instrument, and guarantee status, due within two months of quarter-end. Quarterly domestic and external debt service (amortization and interest payments) are also required within the same timeframe. Additionally, quarterly projections for provincial debt amortization/repayments and interest payments for the subsequent semester are to be submitted at least 30 days before each quarter's end.

outline.title: Eighth Review Under Extended Arrangement: June 2024 Overview
outline.summary: This section introduces the 'EIGHTH REVIEW UNDER THE EXTENDED ARRANGEMENT UNDER THE EXTENDED FUND FACILITY' for Argentina, dated June 10, 2024, outlining its scope including performance criteria modifications, waivers, and a financing assurances review, prepared by the Western Hemisphere Department.

subsections.title: Cover Page and Review Scope: Argentina's EIGHTH REVIEW under EFF, June 10, 2024
subsections.summary: Page 104 is the cover page for Argentina's 'EIGHTH REVIEW UNDER THE EXTENDED ARRANGEMENT UNDER THE EXTENDED FUND FACILITY', dated June 10, 2024. It outlines requests for modification of performance criteria, waivers of nonobservance, and a financing assurances review. It also mentions that the report includes recent developments and was prepared by staff from the Western Hemisphere Department, updating information since the May 31, 2024 Staff Report.

outline.title: Argentina's Economic Performance and Fiscal Consolidation: Q2 2024
outline.summary: This section covers Argentina's economic performance in Q2 2024, detailing improved market indicators, the authorities' strong commitment to macroeconomic stability, and a significant 5% of GDP fiscal consolidation by April 2024, resulting in fiscal surpluses and real term improvements in revenue and expenditure.

subsections.title: Recent Economic Developments and Policy Direction: Q2 2024 Market Indicators
subsections.summary: Page 105 details Argentina's recent economic developments, noting improvements in market indicators since end-2023 despite volatility. It highlights rising spreads and FX gaps, moderated BCRA FX purchases, and positive prospects for Senate approval of fiscal and structural packages. Fiscal targets for end-June are on track, supported by the first positive real tax revenue growth since August 2023.

subsections.title: Argentine Authorities' Commitment and Program Success: Early 2024 Fiscal Adjustment
subsections.summary: Page 106 presents the Argentine authorities' statement, thanking the IMF and affirming their commitment to macroeconomic stability. They report the program is on track with significant overperformance on quantitative targets and fulfilled prior actions.
